findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors
findings.description: Normal cleanup emits error-level messages before and after every batch, including when no rows are found and no error occurred. The count-based and orphan-tag paths do the same. This creates false failure signals and logs potentially large ID lists during routine maintenance. Use debug-level batch summaries without complete ID lists, and reserve error logging for actual failures.

findings.title: SQLite ID-list construction has quadratic allocation cost
findings.description: Each `fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the entire accumulated string. Building a deletion statement therefore requires quadratic copying and allocation as the batch grows—the newly added 32,767 batch-size case exercises this path. This can create substantial CPU and garbage-collection overhead during large cleanups. Build the list with a `strings.Builder` or append integers into a byte buffer, as the existing dashboard-ID filter in this file does.

findings.title: Increasing the global cleanup frequency affects unrelated maintenance jobs
findings.description: Changing the ticker from ten minutes to one minute schedules every cleanup task ten times as often, not just annotation cleanup. This includes temporary-directory scans, dashboard-version deletion, and query-history limit enforcement. The cleanup timeout also remains nine minutes, so a run lasting over a minute can leave a pending tick and trigger another run immediately afterward. Preserve the existing interval unless this broader workload change is intentional and validated; if annotations need a different cadence, schedule them separately.
